executive_summary: The defining thread of today's content is the accelerating crisis of institutional credibility in high-stakes, high-power domains — who controls the future, and whether the people and organizations claiming to lead it can be trusted. The Musk v. Altman trial, now reduced to dueling character assassinations over who betrayed AI's founding mission, exemplifies this breakdown most acutely: the jury is not simply adjudicating a contract dispute but rendering a verdict on which version of Silicon Valley's origin story gets to be canonical. Google's reported inability to compete at the frontier of its own core technology — with DeepMind engineers quietly using rivals' tools — reinforces that even the most resourced institutions are losing credibility through performance failure, not just narrative failure. Together, these two long-form pieces paint a picture of an AI industry where the foundational actors are simultaneously overpromising and underdelivering, eroding the trust necessary for the public and policymakers to grant them the latitude they seek. The California wildfire, while geographically isolated, adds an urgent counterpoint: as climate-driven crises demand rapid, coordinated institutional response, the spectacle of tech's most powerful figures litigating personal grievances over AGI control signals a profound misalignment between where elite attention is focused and where it is most needed.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place foundation model competitor, with a coding deficit severe enough that its own DeepMind engineers reportedly use rivals' tools, even as the company retains a genuine lead in AI for science.
longform.context: Written on the eve of Google I/O 2026, the piece responds to a marked shift in competitive positioning since I/O 2025, when Google was still considered a co-frontrunner; the intervening year saw Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex pull decisively ahead in coding benchmarks, reordering the perceived hierarchy of foundation model labs.
arguments: Google's coding tools have fallen so far behind Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex that DeepMind engineers were 'reportedly fighting over who got access to Claude Code last month,' signaling a structural weakness rather than a temporary lag; a new DeepMind coding team and Nobel laureate John Jumper's involvement suggest Google is taking the crisis seriously, but the author judges a full return to the frontier within the I/O window unlikely.

Science remains Google DeepMind's 'conspicuous strength' and a domain where it shapes the cutting edge: it is the only frontier AI lab with a Nobel Prize, and 2025 releases including the AI co-scientist — described as an 'oracle' by a Stanford scientist — and AlphaEvolve demonstrate a sustained lead that LLM-era AI-for-science has amplified rather than eroded.

Google's health AI ambitions are undercut by a credibility gap: despite conducting strong LLM-based health research, the publicly announced Health Coach targets fitness and diet advice rather than clinical concerns, ceding the health AI narrative to OpenAI's ChatGPT Health and raising the unresolved question of whether this reflects strategic caution or competitive retreat.

Internal and external controversy shadows the conference: 600 employees, many at DeepMind, protested a DoD deal that Sundar Pichai signed the following day, and the concurrent Musk v. Altman trial in Oakland keeps AI governance drama in the foreground, testing whether Demis Hassabis's carefully maintained 'Nobel Prize-winning nerd' persona can insulate Google from the broader industry's reputational turbulence.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it frames Google I/O 2026 not as a product launch event but as a competitive reckoning — the moment when the gap between Google's self-presentation as an AI leader and its actual standing in the most commercially valued capability (coding) becomes publicly undeniable. It also highlights that foundation model competition is bifurcating: coding and consumer AI on one axis, scientific AI on another, with different leaders on each, a dynamic that will shape enterprise and research adoption. The internal protest over the DoD deal signals that workforce dissent, largely dormant since the 2018 Project Maven controversy, has re-emerged as a material reputational and operational risk for Google.
questions_raised: Whether Google's restraint in health AI — deploying a fitness coach rather than a clinical tool — reflects genuine ethical caution or an inability to match OpenAI's execution speed, and what the competitive consequences of that ambiguity will be.

Whether Hassabis's strategy of staying above industry drama is sustainable as Google's own workforce dissent and government contracting decisions pull the company into the same contested terrain that OpenAI and Anthropic already occupy.

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The final week of the Musk v. Altman trial reduced to competing credibility attacks — Altman accused of lying and self-dealing, Musk portrayed as an AGI power-seeker — leaving the jury to adjudicate not just a legal dispute but the foundational narrative of how OpenAI was built and who betrayed its mission.
longform.context: This newsletter dispatch, published May 18, 2026, covers the conclusion of a three-week courtroom trial between Elon Musk and Sam Altman, a case MIT Technology Review has tracked through embedded legal reporter Michelle Kim since week one. The trial centers on OpenAI's contested nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion and Musk's claim that he was deceived about the organization's original purpose.
arguments: Musk's legal team framed him as a victim of institutional bait-and-switch, arguing he co-founded OpenAI under a nonprofit safety mission that Altman later abandoned for commercial gain — but opposing counsel countered that Musk was motivated by control over AGI rather than principle, undermining his standing as an aggrieved idealist.

Altman's credibility was directly attacked through accusations of lying and self-dealing, suggesting his management of OpenAI's transition served personal and financial interests — a charge that, if credited by the jury, would reframe OpenAI's corporate evolution as governance fraud rather than legitimate strategic adaptation.

Trial testimony unearthed previously undisclosed internal culture details — including a 'golden trophy of a donkey's ass' awarded to an employee who challenged Musk — that paint Musk's early involvement as domineering, corroborating the portrait of a founder who sought to control rather than steward the organization.

A secondary story flagged in the same dispatch — Trump trading tech stocks in Nvidia, AMD, Arm, and Palantir ahead of administration policy decisions favorable to each company — places the Musk-Altman trial within a broader pattern of AI-era power concentration and elite actors exploiting regulatory proximity for financial gain.
longform.significance: The case forces a public legal reckoning over whether OpenAI's nonprofit origins created binding obligations or were merely aspirational branding, a question with direct implications for how AI labs can restructure themselves going forward. The jury's verdict will either validate Musk's narrative that safety-mission AI organizations can be captured by commercial interests, or affirm Altman's position that adaptive governance is legitimate — setting a precedent for the entire sector. Coming alongside SpaceX's imminent $1.75 trillion IPO and Chinese AI groups outpacing US rivals in video generation, the trial is one node in a rapidly consolidating power struggle over who controls the infrastructure and narrative of artificial general intelligence.
questions_raised: If the jury sides with Musk on the self-dealing claims, what legal mechanism would actually compel OpenAI to reverse or restructure its for-profit conversion — and does existing nonprofit law have the teeth to enforce it?

The article does not resolve whether Musk's own xAI venture, which Week 1 coverage noted 'distills OpenAI's models,' undermines his claimed fidelity to the original nonprofit safety mission, leaving open the question of whether his lawsuit is principled or purely competitive.
